title: Parameter Calibration for Reduced-Bandwidth Two-Photon Waveguide-QED Simulations
abstract: Waveguide-QED platforms represent one potential approach to scalable quantum technologies, but their simulation remains computationally demanding due to the large number of frequency modes required to describe traveling photons. In practice, increasing the simulated bandwidth rapidly raises the numerical cost, leading to a trade-off between accuracy and tractability. The existing approaches formulated in time-domain indirectly control this trade-off through the choice of time step, which obscures the connection between discretization parameters and the represented spectral window. In this work, we introduce an end-to-end framework to explicitly control the effective bandwidth in waveguide-QED simulations of two-photon scattering. We show that truncating the frequency domain requires consistent shifts of the model parameters, and derive a systematic calibration procedure that preserves the physical accuracy of the reduced model. This enables tuning the central frequency and the bandwidth of the numerical spectrum, leading to a several-fold reduction in the Hilbert space dimension while maintaining physical accuracy. We discuss the limitations of this calibration and relate the finite-bandwidth viewpoint to time-domain discretizations.
summary: This paper addresses the computational bottleneck in waveguide QED simulations caused by large frequency bandwidths. The authors introduce an end-to-end framework that explicitly controls the spectral window and derives a systematic calibration procedure. This method drastically reduces simulation dimensionality while maintaining high physical accuracy, enabling deeper studies of two-photon quantum phenomena.
main_problem: Waveguide-QED simulations are computationally prohibitive because simulating a large bandwidth requires an exponentially increasing number of frequency modes, creating a trade-off between accuracy and computational tractability.
main_result: The authors developed a systematic calibration procedure that allows explicit control over the effective spectral bandwidth, enabling a significant reduction in the required Hilbert space dimension while preserving physical accuracy for two-photon scattering simulations.
method: They transitioned from time-domain simulation methods (constrained by time step $\Delta t$) to an end-to-end frequency-domain framework. This allowed them to derive and apply parameter shifts that compensate for spectral truncation effects.
model_or_system: The system is Waveguide Quantum Electrodynamics (QED), involving a two-level emitter coupled to photons confined in one-dimensional waveguides. The simulation focuses on the two-photon scattering process using an effective Hamiltonian approach.
key_observables: Coincidence probability ($C$), relative error ($	ext{RE}$) compared to theoretical benchmarks, and the spectral profile of the coincidence probability.
important_parameters: The central frequency ($\omega_{	ext{ref}}$) and the effective bandwidth ($\Lambda$) are key tunable parameters. The simulation is benchmarked against monochromatic limits.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a Markovian regime for simplicity, and the calibration procedure primarily corrects the linear component of the two-photon response, potentially neglecting higher-order multi-photon contributions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the convergence of coincidence probability after applying the calibration procedure across various central frequencies ($\omega_{	ext{ref}}$) and show spectral profile comparisons with and without correction as a function of incoming photon frequency.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the computational bottleneck in QED simulations. It then introduces the frequency-domain framework, detailing how bandwidth truncation is implemented. The core contribution is presenting and validating the systematic calibration algorithm (Alg. 1) to restore physical accuracy across varying spectral windows.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial numerical tool for simulating complex quantum light-matter interactions in engineered platforms like waveguides, allowing researchers to explore physics regimes previously limited by computational resources.
